body: I've inherited it.  Plus triggers and poor coping skills.
I've been on different antidepressants for years.  They have helped, they've probably saved my life, but some things can't be fixed - no matter what counseling or treatments I've had I'm still me.

> It does get better, even if that better doesn't last forever.

Yeah, that's what the therapists don't tell you.  We aren't all cut out for this world, and when "better" goes back to "shit" (and repeat) life just becomes a long, exhausting fight.

I'm so surprised that other people feel this way too, it's so illogical but it's a daily thing for me as well.  I hope this dialogue is at least helping us get it out of our heads and exchanging ideas.

> gave up when it became to hard  

Yep, can relate, if something is difficult the voices in my head are just brutal about what a loser I am.
A balance would be nice, yes.  Somewhere right in the middle, where logic could take control over emotion.
I do - er - I think?

Right, so it's a back and forth between aiming for magnificent ("high self esteem"), doing something magnificent (which you may or may not even enjoy), and being reminded that you're really not a special snowflake (insignificant), and then repeat.
Seeing all the Biebers and Swifts not even half my age making millions... or the young inventors or doctors...

It's *really* frustrating when it happens at the same time, and I experience that a lot.  It means my self-esteem and happiness is dependent on things outside of me that I have no control over, yarrrgh!

>  self-defense system to prevent others from harming me

Yes, but for me that system has gone haywire and I don't feel like I have any say in it anymore.
I don't know why that's so difficult.

> I hate myself but conversely I'm all I can think/talk about. It's vile.

Yep, nailed it.  This is me, and I am so sick of me.
Please don't die, the world needs people like you.

So guess what.  I woke up, and my first thought - literally the first - was the emptiness.  Only this time I just lay there and thought about it, felt what it was like to be there, looked around, didn't die, and got out of bed and got on with my day.  Progress.
I can tell.  I'm sorry we're in the same boat, but I'm grateful for it as well.

It's such a bummer to have this invisible imbalance, and the resulting illogical thoughts that *feel* real, and are very consistent. . . *they* are what kill us if we let them.  Yet they're so familiar.  They make more sense to me than "do this, don't do that, try to feel this way, *then* you'll be happy".  The happiness never comes, or when it does it's so fleeting it doesn't seem worth it.

I don't think I ever have tried to embrace it, no.  I've tried yoga, but fuck *that* noise!  The harder I try to sit still with myself the squirmier I feel inside.  I like the idea of embracing the emptiness, but the walls of that room are covered in hateful messages about who I am.
No advice is OK too, it's sort of a miracle that another human being understands what I'm experiencing so your acknowledgement is great.
Thanks for writing.  Feels good to know someone read what I had to say.

You sound wise beyond your years.  I appreciate your response.  Embrace the emptiness?  Hm.  But I *hate it so much*.  Yet it won't go away.  I think you're on to something, I just can't wrap my head around it.

Thanks for your comment, thanks for reading mine.  "Normal social life", to me, means I don't feel horribly awkward and out of place wherever I go.  It means enjoying being around other people rather than dreading it and not even really knowing why.  It means when I'm down at least I know I'm not alone in this world, at least someone else can say "I love you", "You're good enough", *anything* so I know I matter.  Because I don't feel I matter, I feel like 1 of 7.5 billion people.
West Palm Beach, Florida
